enriched.title: Have/Has Been to x Gone to + Simple Future
enriched.summary: Aula sobre a diferença entre 'been to' e 'gone to', contrações (he's, won't) e uso do Simple Future. Inclui muitos exemplos práticos para treinar preenchimento com 'have/has been to' e 'have/has gone to'.
mainTopics: Difference: have/has been to vs have/has gone to
Vocabulário de lugares e atividades (museum, supermarket, spa, etc.)

vocabulary.definition: Verb form used to talk about decisions, predictions or future facts using 'will' + base verb.
examples: A few ships will probably cross the Strait of Hormuz in the medium-term.

vocabulary.definition: A large vessel for transport by sea.
examples: A few ships will probably cross the Strait of Hormuz in the medium-term.

vocabulary.definition: To go from one side to the other of something (e.g., a river, street, or strait).
examples: A few ships will probably cross the Strait of Hormuz in the medium-term.

vocabulary.definition: A narrow passage of water between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman; proper noun.
examples: A few ships will probably cross the Strait of Hormuz in the medium-term.

vocabulary.definition: An intermediate time period between short-term and long-term.
examples: A few ships will probably cross the Strait of Hormuz in the medium-term.

vocabulary.translation: HE IS / HE HAS (Ele é/está / Ele tem - contração)
vocabulary.definition: Contraction for 'he is' or 'he has' depending on context.
examples: HE’S = HE IS / HE HAS
He’s gone to the post office, but he should be back in ten minutes.

vocabulary.definition: Contraction for 'will not', used to form the negative of 'will'.
examples: He’s gone to a meeting and won't be back for an hour.

vocabulary.translation: esteve em / já foi a (e voltou)
vocabulary.definition: 'Have/has been to' indicates someone visited a place and has returned (experience or completed visit).
examples: I know the way to the museum. I’VE BEEN there many times before.
I’VE BEEN TO Japan, but I’ve never visited South Korea.
HAVE you BEEN TO the beach recently?
We’VE BEEN TO that new Italian restaurant twice this month.

vocabulary.definition: 'Have/has gone to' indicates someone went somewhere and is still there (movement, not returned).
examples: She’s gone to the supermarket to buy some milk.
They’ve gone to the cinema.
He’s gone to the post office, but he should be back in ten minutes.

vocabulary.definition: A building where objects of historical, scientific, artistic, or cultural interest are exhibited.
examples: I know the way to the museum. I’VE BEEN there many times before.

vocabulary.definition: A large self-service store selling foods and household goods.
examples: She’s gone to the supermarket to buy some milk.

vocabulary.definition: A place where films/movies are shown to the public.
examples: My parents aren't answering the house phone. I think they’ve gone to the cinema.

vocabulary.definition: A public department or building where postal services are provided.
examples: He’s gone to the post office, but he should be back in ten minutes.

vocabulary.definition: A place offering health and beauty treatments such as massages, facials, and baths.
examples: I’m so well-rested! I’VE BEEN the spa for the whole weekend.

vocabulary.definition: A darker skin color after exposure to the sun or tanning products.
examples: You look tan! Have you been to the beach recently?

vocabulary.definition: Feeling refreshed and having had enough sleep or relaxation.
examples: I’m so well-rested! I’VE BEEN the spa for the whole weekend.

vocabulary.definition: A place where books and other materials are available for reading, study, or borrowing.
examples: No, he’s gone to the library to study for his finals.

vocabulary.definition: End-of-term examinations in a school or university course.
examples: No, he’s gone to the library to study for his finals.

vocabulary.definition: A restaurant specializing in Italian cuisine.
examples: We’ve been to that new Italian restaurant twice this month. The food is excellent!

vocabulary.definition: A public green area in a town, used for recreation.
examples: Where are the children? — They __________ the park to play football.

vocabulary.definition: Informal short form for 'doctor's office' (where a doctor sees patients).
examples: I'm sorry I'm late. I __________ the doctor's for a check-up.

vocabulary.definition: A medical examination to ensure that someone is healthy.
examples: I'm sorry I'm late. I __________ the doctor's for a check-up.

vocabulary.definition: A financial institution where people deposit money, withdraw cash, and do financial transactions.
examples: Have you seen Mary today? — Yes, she __________ the bank, but she’s back in her office now.

vocabulary.definition: A place where people get haircuts and other hair treatments.
examples: Alice is very happy because she __________ the hair salon today. Do you like her new style?

vocabulary.definition: To go shopping to purchase milk (everyday shopping phrase).
examples: She’s gone to the supermarket to buy some milk.

vocabulary.definition: To return to a place.
examples: He’s gone to the post office, but he should be back in ten minutes.
They’ve gone to France for two weeks and will be back on Monday.

vocabulary.definition: People living near you.
examples: My neighbors aren't home. They’ve gone to France for two weeks and will be back on Monday.

grammar.explanation: Uses 'will' + base verb to express predictions, spontaneous decisions, promises or future facts. In the example, 'A few ships will probably cross the Strait of Hormuz' expresses a prediction.
rules: Form: subject + will + base verb (e.g., 'ships will cross').
Use for predictions or likelihoods (often with adverbs like 'probably').
Negative: subject + will not / won't + base verb (e.g., 'won't be back').
examples: A few ships will probably cross the Strait of Hormuz in the medium-term.
He’s gone to a meeting and won't be back for an hour.
commonMistakes: Using 'will' for scheduled events that should use present continuous or 'be going to' (e.g., 'The train leaves at 6' is better than 'The train will leave at 6').
Confusing 'won't' meaning with other negative forms (e.g., 'don't' vs 'won't').

grammar.topic: Have/Has been to vs Have/Has gone to
grammar.explanation: 'Have/has been to' indicates someone visited a place and has returned (experience or completed action). 'Have/has gone to' indicates someone went somewhere and is still there (movement).
rules: 'Have/has been to' = visited (and returned) or experienced (e.g., 'I’ve been to Japan').
'Have/has gone to' = went and is still there / hasn't returned yet (e.g., 'She’s gone to the supermarket').
Use contraction forms as in the examples: 'I’ve been', 'they’ve gone'.
examples: I’VE BEEN there many times before.
She’S GONE TO the supermarket to buy some milk.
My parents aren't answering the house phone. I think they’VE GONE TO the cinema.
I’VE BEEN TO Japan, but I’ve never visited South Korea.
commonMistakes: Saying 'He’s been to the supermarket' when the person is still there (should be 'He’s gone to the supermarket').

grammar.explanation: Contractions combine pronouns with auxiliary verbs in speech/writing. Context determines meaning: 'he's' can be 'he is' or 'he has'.
rules: 'He’s' = 'He is' or 'He has' depending on the verb following or the sentence meaning.
'I've' = 'I have' (present perfect or possession in some contexts).
examples: He’s gone to a meeting and won't be back for an hour.
I’VE BEEN the spa for the whole weekend.
commonMistakes: Avoiding contractions in formal writing when inappropriate.

expressions.usage: Used with have/has + been + to + place to indicate experience of visiting.
examples: I’VE BEEN there many times before.
I’VE BEEN TO Japan, but I’ve never visited South Korea.
HAVE you BEEN TO the beach recently?

expressions.meaning: went to and is still there
expressions.usage: Used with have/has + gone + to + place when the person went and hasn't returned yet.
examples: She’S GONE TO the supermarket to buy some milk.
They’VE GONE TO the cinema.

expressions.usage: Used to indicate someone will return to a place (often with time reference).
examples: He’s gone to the post office, but he should be back in ten minutes.
They’ve gone to France for two weeks and will be back on Monday.

expressions.usage: Common everyday phrase indicating a short shopping errand.
examples: She’s gone to the supermarket to buy some milk.

expressions.usage: Describes someone who has rested enough.
examples: I’m so well-rested! I’VE BEEN the spa for the whole weekend.

practiceQuestions.question: Where are the children? — They __________ the park to play football.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The children went to the park and are presumably still there, so use 'have gone to'.

practiceQuestions.question: I'm sorry I'm late. I __________ the doctor's for a check-up.
practiceQuestions.explanation: If the speaker already returned and is apologizing for being late, use 'have been to' (completed visit).

practiceQuestions.question: Have you seen Mary today? — Yes, she __________ the bank, but she’s back in her office now.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Mary went to the bank and has already returned, so 'has been to' is correct (completed action).

practiceQuestions.question: Alice is very happy because she __________ the hair salon today. Do you like her new style?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Alice went to the hair salon and (context implies) has returned with a new style, so use 'has been to'.

practiceQuestions.question:
Multiple choice: Which sentence is correct if John is still at the office?
A) John has been to the office.
B) John has gone to the office.
practiceQuestions.answer: B) John has gone to the office.
practiceQuestions.explanation: 'Has gone to' indicates John went to the office and is still there. 'Has been to' would imply he already returned.
practiceQuestions.tense: Present Perfect (have/has gone to / have/has been to)

culturalNotes: The Strait of Hormuz is an important and strategic waterway; using it as an example adds real-world topicality to predictions in the Simple Future.

Visits to places like 'spa', 'Italian restaurant' or 'cinema' reflect common leisure activities in English-speaking contexts; 'I've been to' often marks experience, commonly used when sharing travel or leisure experiences.
studyTips: Practice distinguishing 'have/has been to' (experience/completed visit) and 'have/has gone to' (movement/still there) with short role-plays (e.g., one student asks 'Where's Mary?' and the other replies).
Listen for contractions in spoken English: 'he's' can be 'he is' or 'he has' — use context to decide. Practice by converting contracted dialogues to full forms and back.
Make flashcards with place vocabulary (museum, supermarket, post office, etc.) combined with either 'been to' or 'gone to' to reinforce correct pairing.
When forming predictions with 'will', include adverbs like 'probably' to sound natural ('will probably cross').

Fill in the blanks with the correct form of have/has been to or have/has gone to. (Preencha as lacunas com a forma correta de have/has been to ou have/has gone to.)
I know the way to the museum. I’VE BEEN there many times before. (Eu sei o caminho para o museu. Eu ESTIVE lá muitas vezes antes.)
A: Where is your sister? She isn't in her room. B: She’S GONE TO the supermarket to buy some milk. (A: Onde está sua irmã? Ela não está no quarto. B: Ela FOI AO supermercado comprar leite.)
My parents aren't answering the house phone. I think they’VE GONE TO the cinema. (Meus pais não estão atendendo o telefone de casa. Acho que ELES FORAM AO cinema.)
A: "Where is Mark?" B: "He’S GONE TO the post office, but he should be back in ten minutes." (A: "Onde está o Mark?" B: "Ele FOI AO correio, mas deve voltar em dez minutos.")
I’VE BEEN TO Japan, but I’ve never visited South Korea. (EU JÁ FUI AO Japão, mas nunca visitei a Coreia do Sul.)

A: Can I speak to Mr. Thompson? B: I'm afraid not. He’S GONE TO a meeting and won't be back for an hour. (A: Posso falar com o Sr. Thompson? B: Temo que não. Ele FOI A uma reunião e não voltará por uma hora.)
You look tan! HAVE you BEEN TO the beach recently? (Você está bronzeado! Você FOI À praia recentemente?)
My neighbors aren't home. They’VE GONE TO France for two weeks and will be back on Monday. (Meus vizinhos não estão em casa. ELES FORAM À França por duas semanas e voltarão na segunda-feira.)
I’m so well-rested! I’VE BEEN the spa for the whole weekend. (Estou tão descansado! Eu FUI AO spa durante todo o fim de semana.)
A: Is Tom here? B: No, he’S GONE TO the library to study for his finals. (A: O Tom está aqui? B: Não, ele FOI À biblioteca para estudar para os exames finais.)
We’VE BEEN TO that new Italian restaurant twice this month. The food is excellent! (Nós FOMOS Àquele novo restaurante italiano duas vezes este mês. A comida é excelente!)
Where are the children? — They __________ the park to play football. (Onde estão as crianças? — Elas __________ o parque para jogar futebol.)
I'm sorry I'm late. I __________ the doctor's for a check-up. (Sinto muito pelo atraso. Eu __________ ao consultório do médico para um check-up.)
Have you seen Mary today? — Yes, she __________ the bank, but she’s back in her office now. (Você viu a Mary hoje? — Sim, ela __________ o banco, mas ela já voltou para o escritório.)

Alice is very happy because she __________ the hair salon today. Do you like her new style? (Alice está muito feliz porque ela __________ o salão de cabeleireiro hoje. Você gosta do novo estilo dela?)
